difficultyReason: Scientific/methodological argument requiring the test-taker to identify a load-bearing assumption about instrument capability and rule out an alternative explanation. Trap choices include one that superficially supports the field of study rather than the specific conclusion, and one that introduces a plausible but irrelevant historical detail.
stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a Bronze Age settlement in central Anatolia found no traces of iron tools at any stratum dated before 1200 BCE, despite conducting an extensive survey of all known habitation layers. Because iron corrodes more slowly in arid conditions than in humid ones, and the site's soil is notably dry, any iron tools present should have survived long enough to leave detectable remnants. The archaeologists therefore concluded that the inhabitants of this settlement did not use iron tools before 1200 BCE.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron artifacts from the same period have been successfully recovered at other Bronze Age sites located in regions with similarly arid soil conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The settlement was occupied continuously from approximately 2500 BCE until its abandonment around 1150 BCE.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bronze tools found at the site show sophisticated craftsmanship consistent with a culture capable of working with multiple metals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron smelting technology was known to have existed in neighboring regions before 1200 BCE.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Archaeologists have used the same excavation methods at dozens of other Bronze Age sites throughout the eastern Mediterranean.

explanations.correct: The argument's key assumption is that iron tools, if present, would have survived and been detectable in this site's arid soil. Choice A confirms this assumption by establishing that iron artifacts from the same era have in fact been found at other sites with similarly arid conditions — directly showing that the detection method works and that absence of evidence is genuinely evidence of absence here. This closes the gap between 'no iron found' and 'no iron used.'
explanations.A: Correct. Rules out the alternative explanation that the dry conditions somehow still failed to preserve iron; confirms the load-bearing premise that iron would have survived in this soil type.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant trap. The continuous occupation timeline tells us the site was inhabited throughout the relevant period, but it doesn't address whether iron tools would have been detectable if they existed. This does not strengthen the no-iron-tools conclusion.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion trap. The sophistication of bronze craftsmanship might suggest the culture was metallurgically advanced, but it says nothing about whether iron was or wasn't used — a culture capable of working multiple metals could include or exclude iron.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative explanation / opposite answer trap. Knowing that iron smelting existed nearby before 1200 BCE makes it more plausible that the inhabitants could have acquired iron tools, which actually weakens the argument by suggesting the absence is surprising and in need of further explanation.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison trap. That the same excavation methods were used at other sites tells us nothing about whether those methods are sensitive enough to detect iron remnants in this specific arid environment, nor does it confirm the conclusion about this settlement's inhabitants.
